title: Common normal constants and induction of finite semilinear scheme actions
statement: Let $e$ be a field [def-weil-field], and let $I$ be a nonempty finite set. For each $i\in I$ let $F_i/e$ be a finite field extension [def-pc-field-extension] [def-pc-field-tower], let a finite group $J_i$ act on $F_i$ by $e$-automorphisms, and let $V_i$ be a finite-type $F_i$-scheme with a compatible semilinear $J_i$-action. Let $B_i$ be an $e$-scheme and $v_i:V_i\to B_i$ a $J_i$-invariant $e$-morphism [def-pc-scheme] [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. There are a finite normal extension $K/e$ with embeddings $F_i\hookrightarrow K$, a finite group $G$ with a surjection $G\to A=\operatorname{Aut}_e(K)$, and subgroups $\Gamma_i\leq G$ with surjections $\Gamma_i\to J_i$. The two actions on $F_i$ agree, so $\Gamma_i$ acts diagonally on $W_i=V_i\times_{F_i}K$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. The extension $K^G/e$ is purely inseparable. The induced scheme $Y_i=G\times^{\Gamma_i}W_i$ exists: it is the disjoint union of copies of $W_i$ indexed by left cosets of $\Gamma_i$, with scalar structure on the copy represented by $g$ twisted by the image of $g$ in $A$; the relation is $(g\gamma,w)\sim(g,\gamma w)$. Left multiplication gives a semilinear $G$-action, and $[g,w]\mapsto v_i(\operatorname{pr}_1w)$ defines an invariant $e$-morphism $Y_i\to B_i$. For every geometric point $b:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to B_i$ of $B_i$ [def-weil-geometric-point], if the underlying points of the geometric fibre $V_i\times_{B_i}\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ of $v_i$ at $b$ form a nonempty single $J_i$-orbit, then the underlying points of the geometric fibre $Y_i\times_{B_i}\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ of $Y_i\to B_i$ at $b$ form a nonempty single $G$-orbit. If $v_i$ sends every generic point to a generic point with finite residue extension, the same is true of $Y_i\to B_i$. Finite morphisms and generic points use [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], [def-sc-generic-point], [def-weil-residue-field]; geometric fibres use [def-weil-geometric-fibre]. Normal for a finite field extension means that every irreducible polynomial over $e$ with a root in $K$ splits in $K$; no separability is assumed.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.150, contracted products and diagram (2.b). Agent-formulated finite-family semilinear version: take a common finite normal K/e and use the groups of compatible pairs in Aut_e(K) times J_i before induction. This formulation makes the common field and its action explicit; it is a general induction construction, with no alteration, resolution or SNC existence conclusion.

proof.text: Enumerate the finite family. Construct finite extensions $L_r/e$ containing the first $r$ fields: start with $L_0=e$; put $L_r$ and $F_{r+1}$ in a common field and replace that field by their compositum. The compositum degree bound gives $[L_{r+1}:L_r]\leq[F_{r+1}:e]$, so $L_{r+1}/e$ is finite (multiply spanning sets along the tower). Apply the finite normal-extension lemma to the final $L_r/e$, obtaining a finite normal $K/e$ and the required embeddings $F_i\hookrightarrow K$. Identify each $F_i$ with its image.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2 p.150, common constants before induction; finite-family elaboration using Fields 0H7K, 09ID, 09DT.

proof.text: Put $A=\operatorname{Aut}_e(K)$. It is finite: choose a finite $e$-basis of $K$; an automorphism is determined by the images of these basis elements, each of which must be a root of its nonzero minimal polynomial, so there are finitely many choices. Put $G=A\times\prod_{j\in I}J_j$, with its surjection $\pi:G\to A$. Define $\Gamma_i=\{(a,(j_t)_t):a|_{F_i}=j_i\}$. Compatibility is preserved under multiplication and inversion, hence this is a subgroup. Its map to $J_i$ is surjective: given $j\in J_i$, lift the $e$-automorphism of $F_i$ by which $j$ acts (the action need not be faithful) to $a\in A$ by the intermediate-isomorphism lifting lemma, and take $(a,(j_t)_t)$ with $j_i=j$ and all other $j_t=1$. No normality of $F_i/e$ is used. The action of $G$ on $K$ has image $A$, so $K^G=K^A$; the normal fixed-field lemma makes this extension of $e$ purely inseparable.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2 p.150, graph enlargement of finite groups; Fields 0BME(2), 030M(2) for the common-normal-field version.

proof.text: Fix $i$, and abbreviate $\Gamma=\Gamma_i$, $V=V_i$, $F=F_i$, $B=B_i$. Form $W=V\times_F K$. For $\gamma=(a,(j_t))\in\Gamma$, the actions of $j_i$ on $V$ and $a$ on $K$ agree over $F$, so the fibre-product universal property gives an automorphism $\gamma_W$ of $W$. Uniqueness gives $(\gamma\delta)_W=\gamma_W\delta_W$ and $1_W=\mathrm{id}$. Use the convention that a left action by field automorphisms induces $a\mapsto\operatorname{Spec}(a^{-1})$ on the base scheme. Thus if $p:W\to\operatorname{Spec}K$, then $p\gamma_W=\operatorname{Spec}(a^{-1})p$. This is precisely the diagonal semilinear action required by the statement.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2 p.150, equivariant scalar extension in diagram (2.b); explicit universal-property construction.

proof.text: Choose representatives $s(c)$ of the left cosets $c\in G/\Gamma$, with $s(\Gamma)=1$, and form the coproduct $Y=\coprod_c W_c$ in schemes. On the copy represented by $g=s(c)$ give the scalar structure $p_g=\operatorname{Spec}(\pi(g)^{-1})p$. This represents the contracted product: replace an arbitrary pair $(g\gamma,w)$ by $(g,\gamma_Ww)$. The two scalar structures agree, since $p_g\gamma_W=\operatorname{Spec}(\pi(g)^{-1})\operatorname{Spec}(\pi(\gamma)^{-1})p=\operatorname{Spec}((\pi(g)\pi(\gamma))^{-1})p=p_{g\gamma}$. Each pair has a unique representative in a chosen copy, and changing representatives gives these scheme isomorphisms, which compose by the action law. Consequently this finite coproduct realizes the relation $(g\gamma,w)\sim(g,\gamma w)$ as a scheme, without any quotient-existence hypothesis on $V$.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2 p.150, contracted products before (2.b); explicit coset construction with Schemes 01JB–01JC.

proof.text: For $h\in G$ and $g=s(c)$ write $hg=s(hc)\gamma(h,c)$. On the copy $c$ send $w$ to $\gamma(h,c)_Ww$ in the copy $hc$; the coproduct universal property makes this a scheme morphism $h_Y$. The identity $\gamma(h_2h_1,c)=\gamma(h_2,h_1c)\gamma(h_1,c)$ proves the group law, and $h^{-1}_Y$ is the inverse. For semilinearity the scalar structure of its value is $p_{s(hc)}\gamma(h,c)_W=p_{hg}=\operatorname{Spec}(\pi(h)^{-1})p_g$. Thus the action is left multiplication on classes $[g,w]$ and is semilinear for $\pi$.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2 p.150, induced actions in (2.b); coset cocycle and scalar calculation.

proof.text: On each copy of $W$ use $q=v_i\operatorname{pr}_1:W\to B$. It is $\Gamma$-invariant because $v_i$ is $J_i$-invariant. The coproduct universal property gives $Y\to B$. The relation changes $w$ by an element of $\Gamma$, so the formula $[g,w]\mapsto v_i(\operatorname{pr}_1w)$ is well defined. The action just constructed changes the component and applies such an element to $w$, so this map is $G$-invariant. All its maps are over $e$, since each scalar twist fixes $e$.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2 p.150, induced morphisms in (2.b).

proof.text: Let $b:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to B$ be geometric, and suppose the underlying points of $V_b$ form a nonempty single $J_i$-orbit. These points are all $\Omega$-rational. Indeed, $V_b$ is locally of finite type over $\Omega$: on affine charts the algebra $R\otimes_S\Omega$ is generated over $\Omega$ by finite generators of $R/e$, since $V$ is finite type over the finite extension $F/e$. A nonempty finite-type affine chart has a maximal ideal, whose residue field is finite over $\Omega$ by Zariski\textquotesingle s lemma and hence equals $\Omega$. Its $J_i$-translates exhaust $V_b$ and stay rational because the action on the fibre is over $\Omega$. Above each rational $x\in V_b$, the projection $W_b\to V_b$ has fibre $\operatorname{Spec}(\Omega\otimes_{F,x}K)$. This algebra is nonzero and finite-dimensional over $\Omega$ (a basis of $K/F$ remains a basis after tensoring). Its prime quotients are finite-dimensional domains and hence fields; being finite extensions of the algebraically closed $\Omega$, they equal $\Omega$. Its points therefore correspond exactly to embeddings $\alpha:K\hookrightarrow\Omega$ extending the scalar map $F\to\Omega$ of $x$. A maximal ideal proves this set is nonempty, including when the tensor algebra has nilpotents.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2 (2.b), geometric-orbit verification; Algebra 00FV and finite-dimensional algebra argument.

proof.text: The points of $W_b$ form one $\Gamma$-orbit. Given two such points, first choose $j\in J_i$ carrying the first image in $V_b$ to the second and lift $j$ to $\gamma\in\Gamma$. After applying $\gamma$ the two points lie over the same rational $x$. The extension $K/F$ is normal by normality over intermediate fields. Its embeddings in $\Omega$ extending this $F$-structure differ by an element of $\operatorname{Aut}_F(K)$, by the normal-embeddings lemma. Every $a\in\operatorname{Aut}_F(K)$ gives $(a,(1)_t)\in\Gamma$, acting over $V$; on these embeddings its action is $\alpha\mapsto\alpha\circ a^{-1}$. As $a$ ranges through the group, this is transitive on the embeddings. This gives the second move between the two points without assuming separability of $K/F$.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2 p.150, transitive induced fibres; Fields 09HN and 0BR4.

proof.text: Base change the coproduct description along $b$. Its points are the disjoint union of the points in the copies of $W_b$: fibre products distribute over a disjoint open cover, as can be checked by restricting the fibre-product universal property to each open copy. Given two points of $Y_b$, multiply by the inverses of their component representatives to move each into the identity component. There the preceding $\Gamma$-orbit argument joins them. Composing these three elements of $G$ joins the original points. The identity component contains a point by the preceding tensor calculation, so $Y_b$ is nonempty.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2 p.150, contracted product and orbit transfer in (2.b).

proof.text: Finally consider a generic point $y$ of a component of $W$. On an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}R$ of $V$, the projection is $\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_F K)\to\operatorname{Spec}R$. This ring extension is finite free. It is flat because tensoring an $R$-module with it is a finite direct sum of that module, and hence preserves exact sequences. If the prime $\mathfrak q$ of $y$ contracts to $\mathfrak p$ and $\mathfrak p_0\subseteq\mathfrak p$, flat going-down gives $\mathfrak q_0\subseteq\mathfrak q$ above $\mathfrak p_0$. Minimality of $\mathfrak q$ forces equality, hence $\mathfrak p$ is minimal and $x=\operatorname{pr}_1(y)$ is generic in $V$. The algebra $\kappa(x)\otimes_F K$ is finite-dimensional; its quotient at the prime of $y$ is a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field, and equals $\kappa(y)$. Thus $\kappa(y)/\kappa(x)$ is finite. By the hypothesis on $v_i$, $v_i(x)$ is generic in $B_i$ and $\kappa(x)/\kappa(v_i(x))$ is finite; multiplying finite spanning sets proves the same for $\kappa(y)/\kappa(v_i(x))$. The clopen copies in $Y_i$ have exactly the generic points of their copies of $W$; scalar twists do not change the underlying $e$-scheme or the map to $B_i$. This proves the generic-point clause.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2 diagram (2.b), maximal domination and generic finiteness; Algebra 00HS and the finite-dimensional-domain lemma.
